questiontext.text:
For each pair of statements, decide which implications are true.

  1. Where {@ctx1@}: \(P\) is ‘{@P1@}’ and \(Q\) is ‘{@Q1@}’.

    [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

  2. Where {@ctx2@}: \(P\) is ‘{@P2@}’ and \(Q\) is ‘{@Q2@}’.

    [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

  3. Where {@ctx3@}: \(P\) is ‘{@P3@}’ and \(Q\) is ‘{@Q3@}’.

    [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]

  4. Where {@ctx4@}: \(P\) is ‘{@P4@}’ and \(Q\) is ‘{@Q4@}’.

    [[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]] [[feedback:prt4]]

generalfeedback.text:
\(P \Rightarrow Q\) means: whenever \(P\) is true, \(Q\) is true. Its converse is \(Q \Rightarrow P\). To show that an implication is false, one case where the first statement is true and the second is false is enough. \(P \Leftrightarrow Q\) needs both implications.

  1. \(P\): {@P1@}; \(Q\): {@Q1@}. {@labans(cor1)@} {@expl1@}

  2. \(P\): {@P2@}; \(Q\): {@Q2@}. {@labans(cor2)@} {@expl2@}

  3. \(P\): {@P3@}; \(Q\): {@Q3@}. {@labans(cor3)@} {@expl3@}

  4. \(P\): {@P4@}; \(Q\): {@Q4@}. {@labans(cor4)@} {@expl4@}

questiondescription.text: This question is based on the discussion of implication, the converse and if and only if (pp. 9-10) in Section 4 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.
